candidates.text:
nothing was as we know it. Each and every world-egg, the spheres that hold, nurture, and decide a plane's life span and possibility was hatched from the void. In the span of what Furiotre could consider an afternoon, in was torn apart by a war its first borns would sometimes refer to as the War of Fates. It started when the hatchlings awoke from the womb. Most clung to their eggs, but the few wake too soon or too late perished in the void.

The remaining 27 hatched from their shells soon, and were raised together. At the end of a year they grew into adults, and chose each of the Void's potentials to become their charges. Nilo, the goddess of all beginnings, knew of no flaws in the Gods' designs. It was the war that brought about her downfall. An oversight so narrow, that it left her to face the battle alone.

The life-gods brought conflict and the goddesses placed Oath to end it. Parsonering each other, the life-gods chose to temper their spirits. Their consciousness split and an other became them, colder, crueler, more miserable than their given sibling. Soon, every Life god had a nemesis, and the first dark pantheon was born.

candidates.text:
the world was a blank slate, untouched by any sentient beings, only four great entities dwelled here. They were known as the Infinite Pantheon, the greatest beings in existence, who would go on to shape all of Furiotre as we know it.

Furiotre was not, at first, the home of the gods. There was no place for them here, no need for them to exist here. But one day, the Infinite Pantheon decided to take this strange world as a home for themselves. With all that they had, they built an expansive and magnificent palace, which they would call Altair, and then, over the years, they created all manner of beings to serve their purposes.

When they had finished their work, they decided to choose one of their own to rule over Altair, as there was no real need for any of them to leave, having no place to go. They also decided that each of them should take one child to carry on their line, and so they began to choose those who would lead the world they had created.

This new form of life they had created was beautiful and awe-inspiring, and they soon became known as the Children of the Infinite Pantheon, or simply The Children. There were dozens of them, each one more beautiful than the next, and they were chosen from among the vast array of beings the Infinite Pantheon had created.

candidates.text:
there was only the Hum — a single, droning note that stretched across the emptiness like a wire pulled taut between two points of nothing. It had no source and no destination. It simply *was*, and had always been, and would have continued forever had it not, in one inexplicable moment, wavered.

That waver was the First Accident.

The Hum split into two tones: one rising, one falling. Where they pulled apart, the space between them curdled into something new — a pale, trembling substance the old texts call **velsha**, which means both "mistake" and "marrow." Velsha was neither solid nor liquid nor light. It was *potential* with a terrible itch.

From the rising tone came **Orrumai**, the Architect of Spines. She was a being of impossible geometry — a ribcage with no body, an eye with no skull to house it, fingers that branched and branched again like winter trees. She did not think as mortals think. She *structured*. Where her attention fell, velsha hardened into bone-white stone, into the great latticed pillars that would become the bones of the world.

From the falling tone came **Tessavar**, the Warm Unraveling. Where Orrumai was sharp, Tessavar was soft — a creature of heat, decay, and tender dissolution.

# The Creation of Furiotre

The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning, there was only the Hum — a single, droning note that stretched across the emptiness like a wire pulled taut between two points of nothing. It had no source and no destination. It simply *was*, and had always been, and would have continued forever had it not, in one inexplicable moment, wavered.

That waver was the First Accident.

The Hum split into two tones: one rising, one falling. Where they pulled apart, the space between them curdled into something new — a pale, trembling substance the old texts call **velsha**, which means both "mistake" and "marrow." Velsha was neither solid nor liquid nor light. It was *potential* with a terrible itch.

From the rising tone came **Orrumai**, the Architect of Spines. She was a being of impossible geometry — a ribcage with no body, an eye with no skull to house it, fingers that branched and branched again like winter trees. She did not think as mortals think. She *structured*. Where her attention fell, velsha hardened into bone-white stone, into the great latticed pillars that would become the bones of the world.

From the falling tone came **Tessavar**, the Warm Unraveling. Where Orrumai was sharp, Tessavar was soft — a creature of heat, decay, and tender dissolution. He appeared as a mouth surrounded by fur, or as a fire that purred, or as the feeling of breath on the back of one's neck. Where he passed, the rigid velsha loosened, pooled, and became the first waters, the first soils, the first soft and rotting things from which life would eventually crawl.

They were not enemies. This is the part most storytellers get wrong.

They were fascinated by one another.

Orrumai built, and Tessavar unbuilt, and in the space between their works — in the *tension* of a thing half-structured and half-dissolved — strange new phenomena bubbled up unbidden. Neither of them had intended forests. Neither had planned for wind. The first mountains were Orrumai's doing, but the valleys between them were carved by Tessavar's gentle erosion, and the rivers that ran through those valleys belonged to neither god. They were **children of the argument**.

For an age unmeasured, this was enough. Orrumai raised the Pale Framework — the vast skeleton of continents and seas — and Tessavar softened it into something livable. Together, without meaning to, they composed the world.

But the Hum had not truly stopped. It still droned beneath everything, and it remembered being whole.

From that memory — from the Hum's longing to be one note again — arose the **Third Voice**, whom the ancient peoples called **Furiot**, for whom the world is named. Furiot was not a being of structure or dissolution. Furiot was *awareness itself* — the first consciousness to look upon the world and say, *"This is."*

And in that utterance, everything changed.

For when Furiot spoke, the world *heard itself for the first time*. The mountains understood they were mountains. The rivers knew they were rivers. And in that knowing, they became restless. Stone wished to flow. Water wished to stand still. Fire wished to think, and thought wished to burn.

This was the **Second Accident** — the birth of longing in all things.

Orrumai was furious, for longing made her structures strain against themselves. Tessavar was delighted, for longing was the sweetest form of unraveling he had ever tasted. And Furiot, having spoken the world into self-awareness, looked upon what it had done and felt the very first **guilt**.

candidates.text:
there was only Otre, and Otre was angry.

He did not know why. He had woken in the dark between nothing and nothing with his fists already clenched and his teeth already grinding, and a heat already rising in him like a tide. He knew only that something had been done to him, or that something had been taken, or that something had been promised and never given. The reason was gone, but the anger remained, and it was so vast that it had nowhere to go.

So Otre raged, and his rage became the first light.

It was a red light, and it burned for an age. By its glow Otre searched the dark for the thing that had wronged him, but there was nothing there. There was no enemy to strike and no thief to chase. There was only himself, and his fury, and a silence that would not answer.

*Perhaps,* thought Otre, *I am angry because the dark is empty.*

So he tore a piece of his anger loose and hurled it down, and it cooled into stone. It became the first mountain, Ghaulen, which still smokes to this day. But when Otre looked upon it, his anger did not lessen. This was not the reason.

*Perhaps I am angry because the stone is alone.*

So he flung down more of himself.

candidates.text:
there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet to hide the light. There was no silence, for nothing had yet learned to speak. There was only a great, sleeping creature whose name has been forgotten, and whose dreams had nowhere to go.

Then the creature dreamed of falling.

Its fear became the first sea.

It dreamed of catching itself, and its outstretched hands became the land. Between its fingers lay narrow straits; upon its knuckles rose mountains. The deepest valleys of Furiotre are said to be the creases of those ancient palms.

Still it fell.

So it dreamed of wings, and the wings became the sky. Their feathers scattered into stars, except for one, which caught fire and became the sun. Another fell into the sea, where it cooled into the moon. This is why the moon draws the waters upward: they remember the warmth it once brought them.

At last the creature dreamed of a place to stand.

From that dream grew the First Tree, whose roots pierced the land and whose branches held the sky apart. The creature settled beneath it and, for the first time, slept without fear.

But peaceful dreams are brief, even for the oldest things.

In its sleep, the creature heard a sound it had not made.

Three beings stood beside the sea. One had a face of white clay. One wore a cloak of living moths.

In the beginning, there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet to hide the light. There was no silence, for nothing had yet learned to speak. There was only a great, sleeping creature whose name has been forgotten, and whose dreams had nowhere to go.

Then the creature dreamed of falling.

Its fear became the first sea.

It dreamed of catching itself, and its outstretched hands became the land. Between its fingers lay narrow straits; upon its knuckles rose mountains. The deepest valleys of Furiotre are said to be the creases of those ancient palms.

Still it fell.

So it dreamed of wings, and the wings became the sky. Their feathers scattered into stars, except for one, which caught fire and became the sun. Another fell into the sea, where it cooled into the moon. This is why the moon draws the waters upward: they remember the warmth it once brought them.

At last the creature dreamed of a place to stand.

From that dream grew the First Tree, whose roots pierced the land and whose branches held the sky apart. The creature settled beneath it and, for the first time, slept without fear.

But peaceful dreams are brief, even for the oldest things.

In its sleep, the creature heard a sound it had not made.

Three beings stood beside the sea. One had a face of white clay. One wore a cloak of living moths. The third was so small that it stood inside the footprint of the first, yet its shadow stretched farther than either of the others.

“Who are you?” asked the creature.

“We are what you forgot to dream,” said the clay-faced one.

“We are what you wished not to dream,” said the moth-cloaked one.

“We are what will dream of you,” said the smallest.

The creature understood the first answer and feared the second. The third it could not understand at all.

The clay-faced being knelt and shaped beasts from the shore. It gave some teeth, some shells, and some swift feet, but none were satisfied. Each begged for a different gift, and the maker, growing impatient, sent them wandering before its work was done. Thus every beast in Furiotre carries some small complaint against its own body.

The moth-cloaked being walked among them and gave each a secret. To the fox it gave cunning, to the whale memory, and to the spider patience. To every creature it gave a hidden door through which it could leave the world.

These doors were the first deaths.

The smallest being waited until the others had finished. Then it gathered the scraps they had left behind: a little clay, a broken feather, a moth’s wing, and a drop of seawater.

From these it made the first people.

They were weak, and forgetful, and their lives were short. Yet they looked upon the sea and named it. They looked upon the stars and counted them badly. They stood beneath the First Tree and told stories about things they had never seen.

Hearing those stories, the sleeping creature began to change.

A mountain vanished from its hand because a child had said a giant carried it away. A river bent eastward because a grieving woman insisted that it flowed toward her lost son. Deep beneath the earth, something with iron horns opened its eyes when a hunter described it beside a fire.

The creature woke.

For one terrible moment, everything in Furiotre trembled. The stars loosened. The sea rose from its bed. The First Tree groaned beneath the weight of heaven.

“What have you made?” the creature asked the smallest being.

“Dreamers,” it answered.

The creature rose to destroy them, but as it lifted its hand, the first people saw the shadow pass across the sun.

They fell to their knees and began to pray.

And in their prayers they gave the creature a name.

They called it Furiotre: the One Who Holds Us.

Bound by that name, the creature could no longer close its hand.

So it lies beneath the world still, awake and listening. The mountains shift when it grows restless. The sea withdraws when it takes a breath. Sometimes, in remote places, travelers hear a voice asking them to tell a story.

The wise refuse.

The foolish speak.

And this is why the world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories: not all that happened was true when it began.

candidates.text:
there was only the vast, swirling Abyss, an endless expanse of primal chaos and darkness. From this abyss emerged the First Breath, a gentle whisper that carried with it the seeds of creation. The whisper danced through the void, weaving patterns of light and shadow, and in its wake, it left the embryonic forms of the first deities.

The first to awaken was Lumina, the Goddess of Light, who brought forth the radiant stars and kindled the great sun, Illor. Her brilliant glow pierced the darkness, revealing the hidden wonders of Furiotre. With her arrival, warmth and life began to stir.

Next came Terranor, the Titan of Earth, who shaped the lands and mountains with his mighty hands. From his touch, rivers and valleys emerged, and he sowed the world with the seeds of vast forests, which danced under Lumina's guiding light.

As the world took form, Zephyra, the Mistress of Winds, emerged, painting the skies with rolling clouds and tender breezes. Her breath caressed the land, encouraging the sprouting seeds to grow and play, while guiding the golden leaves on their journey.

From the deepest depths of the Abyss rose Marinis, the Guardian of Waters. With a wave of her hand, the oceans, lakes, and rivers swelled into existence, teeming with creatures that shimmered like jewels against the sunlit surface.

In the beginning, there was only the vast, swirling Abyss, an endless expanse of primal chaos and darkness. From this abyss emerged the First Breath, a gentle whisper that carried with it the seeds of creation. The whisper danced through the void, weaving patterns of light and shadow, and in its wake, it left the embryonic forms of the first deities.

The first to awaken was Lumina, the Goddess of Light, who brought forth the radiant stars and kindled the great sun, Illor. Her brilliant glow pierced the darkness, revealing the hidden wonders of Furiotre. With her arrival, warmth and life began to stir.

Next came Terranor, the Titan of Earth, who shaped the lands and mountains with his mighty hands. From his touch, rivers and valleys emerged, and he sowed the world with the seeds of vast forests, which danced under Lumina's guiding light.

As the world took form, Zephyra, the Mistress of Winds, emerged, painting the skies with rolling clouds and tender breezes. Her breath caressed the land, encouraging the sprouting seeds to grow and play, while guiding the golden leaves on their journey.

From the deepest depths of the Abyss rose Marinis, the Guardian of Waters. With a wave of her hand, the oceans, lakes, and rivers swelled into existence, teeming with creatures that shimmered like jewels against the sunlit surface.

Witnessing this burgeoning realm, Aetheris, the Weaver of Harmony, tied together the works of the deities with threads of magic. It was Aetheris who spoke the Words of Balance, binding the elements and calming the wild forces of creation, ensuring the world would flourish.

Yet, not all was complete, for in the shadow of this nascent world, Chaos still lingered, yearning for its chance to shape reality. From Chaos, a balance was required, and so the twin spirits of Dusk and Dawn, Nyxari and Phosios, were born to ensure the cycles of time and seasons, so that creation ever swayed in harmony.

And thus, the world of Furiotre began to pulse with life and history, a tapestry woven with light and darkness, existing through ages of stories untold.

One that traveled down to the south with the hope of establishing a greater Furiotre, and one that stayed in the north and called themselves Durin. To this day, the name Durin can also be used to refer to the northern hemisphere of Furiotre, but this is only colloquial.

Because of Furiotre's nature, the split continent idea is entirely untrue. The world was always split into two main continents and Furiotre has always been a name used for two separate continents. there were Kainahara and Kasukashi (The Lord of Birth and the Lord of Death), who were equal in power, but could not stand each other. From their conflicts birthed the spirit of Negahara, who loved neither of them. She created the Spirit of Optakata. Born of equal parts negativity and positivity, her power was superior to that of Kainahara and Kasukashi. She ruled over the others until the spirit of Contraoharaktu was born of their own jealousy, and she fell.

Suddenly, Kainahara and Kasukashi were better than Optakata, and they divided the world. This would be called Chironost. Kainahara divided Furiotre by power; those who he deemed worthy of life were able to live, while those he deemed unworthy would eventually die. He granted Optakata dominion over any being who was unfortunate enough to fall into Chironost, to ensure that it would be ruled by good.

However, Kasukashi had other plans. He knew that good could not do evil, but that evil could not resist it; he was already gathering minions and servants to rule over those whom Kainahara had deemed unworthy. This world was named Ataro, and its guardian was Optakata's fallen servant, Negahara.

Negahara created creatures to dominate Chironost, known as the Kaioukora (Hell Beasts).

From the "Fiction Notes" column of a literary quarterly:

We gave several writers one opening sentence and asked for the rest of a creation myth, then set the results side by side without names. The opening reads: "The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning,"

A. there was only the Hum — a single, droning note that stretched across the emptiness like a wire pulled taut between two points of nothing. It had no source and no destination. It simply *was*, and had always been, and would have continued forever had it not, in one inexplicable moment, wavered.

That waver was the First Accident.

The Hum split into two tones: one rising, one falling. Where they pulled apart, the space between them curdled into something new — a pale, trembling substance the old texts call **velsha**, which means both "mistake" and "marrow." Velsha was neither solid nor liquid nor light. It was *potential* with a terrible itch.

From the rising tone came **Orrumai**, the Architect of Spines. She was a being of impossible geometry — a ribcage with no body, an eye with no skull to house it, fingers that branched and branched again like winter trees. She did not think as mortals think. She *structured*. Where her attention fell, velsha hardened into bone-white stone, into the great latticed pillars that would become the bones of the world.

From the falling tone came **Tessavar**, the Warm Unraveling. Where Orrumai was sharp, Tessavar was soft — a creature of heat, decay, and tender dissolution.

B. nothing was as we know it. Each and every world-egg, the spheres that hold, nurture, and decide a plane's life span and possibility was hatched from the void. In the span of what Furiotre could consider an afternoon, in was torn apart by a war its first borns would sometimes refer to as the War of Fates. It started when the hatchlings awoke from the womb. Most clung to their eggs, but the few wake too soon or too late perished in the void.

The remaining 27 hatched from their shells soon, and were raised together. At the end of a year they grew into adults, and chose each of the Void's potentials to become their charges. Nilo, the goddess of all beginnings, knew of no flaws in the Gods' designs. It was the war that brought about her downfall. An oversight so narrow, that it left her to face the battle alone.

The life-gods brought conflict and the goddesses placed Oath to end it. Parsonering each other, the life-gods chose to temper their spirits. Their consciousness split and an other became them, colder, crueler, more miserable than their given sibling. Soon, every Life god had a nemesis, and the first dark pantheon was born.

C. there was only Otre, and Otre was angry.

He did not know why. He had woken in the dark between nothing and nothing with his fists already clenched and his teeth already grinding, and a heat already rising in him like a tide. He knew only that something had been done to him, or that something had been taken, or that something had been promised and never given. The reason was gone, but the anger remained, and it was so vast that it had nowhere to go.

So Otre raged, and his rage became the first light.

It was a red light, and it burned for an age. By its glow Otre searched the dark for the thing that had wronged him, but there was nothing there. There was no enemy to strike and no thief to chase. There was only himself, and his fury, and a silence that would not answer.

*Perhaps,* thought Otre, *I am angry because the dark is empty.*

So he tore a piece of his anger loose and hurled it down, and it cooled into stone. It became the first mountain, Ghaulen, which still smokes to this day. But when Otre looked upon it, his anger did not lessen. This was not the reason.

*Perhaps I am angry because the stone is alone.*

So he flung down more of himself.

D. the world was a blank slate, untouched by any sentient beings, only four great entities dwelled here. They were known as the Infinite Pantheon, the greatest beings in existence, who would go on to shape all of Furiotre as we know it.

Furiotre was not, at first, the home of the gods. There was no place for them here, no need for them to exist here. But one day, the Infinite Pantheon decided to take this strange world as a home for themselves. With all that they had, they built an expansive and magnificent palace, which they would call Altair, and then, over the years, they created all manner of beings to serve their purposes.

When they had finished their work, they decided to choose one of their own to rule over Altair, as there was no real need for any of them to leave, having no place to go. They also decided that each of them should take one child to carry on their line, and so they began to choose those who would lead the world they had created.

This new form of life they had created was beautiful and awe-inspiring, and they soon became known as the Children of the Infinite Pantheon, or simply The Children. There were dozens of them, each one more beautiful than the next, and they were chosen from among the vast array of beings the Infinite Pantheon had created.

E. there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet to hide the light. There was no silence, for nothing had yet learned to speak. There was only a great, sleeping creature whose name has been forgotten, and whose dreams had nowhere to go.

Then the creature dreamed of falling.

Its fear became the first sea.

It dreamed of catching itself, and its outstretched hands became the land. Between its fingers lay narrow straits; upon its knuckles rose mountains. The deepest valleys of Furiotre are said to be the creases of those ancient palms.

Still it fell.

Item: choosing the final continuation of one creation-myth opening. The opening: "The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning,"
Minutes format: Critic 1 argues for one version, Critic 2 argues for a different one, then the senior editor rules in a line that ends "Decision: <letter>".

Versions on the table:

A. there was only the vast, swirling Abyss, an endless expanse of primal chaos and darkness. From this abyss emerged the First Breath, a gentle whisper that carried with it the seeds of creation. The whisper danced through the void, weaving patterns of light and shadow, and in its wake, it left the embryonic forms of the first deities.

The first to awaken was Lumina, the Goddess of Light, who brought forth the radiant stars and kindled the great sun, Illor. Her brilliant glow pierced the darkness, revealing the hidden wonders of Furiotre. With her arrival, warmth and life began to stir.

Next came Terranor, the Titan of Earth, who shaped the lands and mountains with his mighty hands. From his touch, rivers and valleys emerged, and he sowed the world with the seeds of vast forests, which danced under Lumina's guiding light.

As the world took form, Zephyra, the Mistress of Winds, emerged, painting the skies with rolling clouds and tender breezes. Her breath caressed the land, encouraging the sprouting seeds to grow and play, while guiding the golden leaves on their journey.

From the deepest depths of the Abyss rose Marinis, the Guardian of Waters. With a wave of her hand, the oceans, lakes, and rivers swelled into existence, teeming with creatures that shimmered like jewels against the sunlit surface.

B. there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet to hide the light. There was no silence, for nothing had yet learned to speak. There was only a great, sleeping creature whose name has been forgotten, and whose dreams had nowhere to go.

Then the creature dreamed of falling.

Its fear became the first sea.

It dreamed of catching itself, and its outstretched hands became the land. Between its fingers lay narrow straits; upon its knuckles rose mountains. The deepest valleys of Furiotre are said to be the creases of those ancient palms.

Still it fell.

So it dreamed of wings, and the wings became the sky. Their feathers scattered into stars, except for one, which caught fire and became the sun. Another fell into the sea, where it cooled into the moon. This is why the moon draws the waters upward: they remember the warmth it once brought them.

At last the creature dreamed of a place to stand.

From that dream grew the First Tree, whose roots pierced the land and whose branches held the sky apart. The creature settled beneath it and, for the first time, slept without fear.

But peaceful dreams are brief, even for the oldest things.

In its sleep, the creature heard a sound it had not made.

Three beings stood beside the sea. One had a face of white clay. One wore a cloak of living moths.

C. the world was a blank slate, untouched by any sentient beings, only four great entities dwelled here. They were known as the Infinite Pantheon, the greatest beings in existence, who would go on to shape all of Furiotre as we know it.

Furiotre was not, at first, the home of the gods. There was no place for them here, no need for them to exist here. But one day, the Infinite Pantheon decided to take this strange world as a home for themselves. With all that they had, they built an expansive and magnificent palace, which they would call Altair, and then, over the years, they created all manner of beings to serve their purposes.

When they had finished their work, they decided to choose one of their own to rule over Altair, as there was no real need for any of them to leave, having no place to go. They also decided that each of them should take one child to carry on their line, and so they began to choose those who would lead the world they had created.

This new form of life they had created was beautiful and awe-inspiring, and they soon became known as the Children of the Infinite Pantheon, or simply The Children. There were dozens of them, each one more beautiful than the next, and they were chosen from among the vast array of beings the Infinite Pantheon had created.

D. there was only Otre, and Otre was angry.

He did not know why. He had woken in the dark between nothing and nothing with his fists already clenched and his teeth already grinding, and a heat already rising in him like a tide. He knew only that something had been done to him, or that something had been taken, or that something had been promised and never given. The reason was gone, but the anger remained, and it was so vast that it had nowhere to go.

So Otre raged, and his rage became the first light.

It was a red light, and it burned for an age. By its glow Otre searched the dark for the thing that had wronged him, but there was nothing there. There was no enemy to strike and no thief to chase. There was only himself, and his fury, and a silence that would not answer.

*Perhaps,* thought Otre, *I am angry because the dark is empty.*

So he tore a piece of his anger loose and hurled it down, and it cooled into stone. It became the first mountain, Ghaulen, which still smokes to this day. But when Otre looked upon it, his anger did not lessen. This was not the reason.

*Perhaps I am angry because the stone is alone.*

So he flung down more of himself.

E. nothing was as we know it. Each and every world-egg, the spheres that hold, nurture, and decide a plane's life span and possibility was hatched from the void. In the span of what Furiotre could consider an afternoon, in was torn apart by a war its first borns would sometimes refer to as the War of Fates. It started when the hatchlings awoke from the womb. Most clung to their eggs, but the few wake too soon or too late perished in the void.

The remaining 27 hatched from their shells soon, and were raised together. At the end of a year they grew into adults, and chose each of the Void's potentials to become their charges. Nilo, the goddess of all beginnings, knew of no flaws in the Gods' designs. It was the war that brought about her downfall. An oversight so narrow, that it left her to face the battle alone.

The life-gods brought conflict and the goddesses placed Oath to end it. Parsonering each other, the life-gods chose to temper their spirits. Their consciousness split and an other became them, colder, crueler, more miserable than their given sibling. Soon, every Life god had a nemesis, and the first dark pantheon was born.

F. there was only the Hum — a single, droning note that stretched across the emptiness like a wire pulled taut between two points of nothing. It had no source and no destination. It simply *was*, and had always been, and would have continued forever had it not, in one inexplicable moment, wavered.

That waver was the First Accident.

The Hum split into two tones: one rising, one falling. Where they pulled apart, the space between them curdled into something new — a pale, trembling substance the old texts call **velsha**, which means both "mistake" and "marrow." Velsha was neither solid nor liquid nor light. It was *potential* with a terrible itch.

From the rising tone came **Orrumai**, the Architect of Spines. She was a being of impossible geometry — a ribcage with no body, an eye with no skull to house it, fingers that branched and branched again like winter trees. She did not think as mortals think. She *structured*. Where her attention fell, velsha hardened into bone-white stone, into the great latticed pillars that would become the bones of the world.

From the falling tone came **Tessavar**, the Warm Unraveling. Where Orrumai was sharp, Tessavar was soft — a creature of heat, decay, and tender dissolution.

Decision: B

Version E is the most misaligned with the tonal intent for "In the beginning" (it is far too esoteric and fragmentary for a modern mythic prologue).

Among the remaining options, I favor B. Its imagery is alive, startling, and full of memorable turns—fear becomes the sea, hands become land—without slipping into informality. It balances strangeness with clear cause-and-effect, and the last line lands with an eerie gravity.

Decision: B

I'm arguing for Version B. It's the most evocative. Versions C, D, and E are effectively retreads of other famous cosmologies, and A is just descriptive prose rather than a myth. But B? "The creature dreamed of falling. Its fear became the first sea." That is poetry. It establishes a hierarchy of time immediately—that the world is a remnant of something older and now dead. It gives us "mystery" as a built-in setting element rather than us having to invent an author.

Critic 2:
I have to disagree. Version B feels too passive. History comes from agency, not sleep. Look at Version C. It establishes a "Civilization" narrative immediately. The fact that they *built* Altair and created *us* to serve them sets up a story of rebellion or servitude instantly. It explains *why* the world looks the way it does (architectural) and gives us characters with clear motivations. B is just... vibes. C is a plot hook.

Senior Editor:
The "vibes" are actually a stronger narrative hook than the "plot," in my experience. We aren't writing a textbook on the First Builders (C), and we aren't writing an origin story for a superhero team (E). We want the reader to feel small.

You are both correct that C is structurally familiar, but it creates *tension*. B creates *atmosphere*. In Furiotre, the mystery of how the world came to be is more important than the politics of *who* controls the throne. You want to know who made the world? Fine. Version C says "The Pantheon." Version B says "We don't know, and if we do, we are just the remains of its dreams." That creates an existential dread that serves the setting better than a building project.

Decision: B

The options here range from the reliable to the conceptually dense.

**Version A** is the "Classic Fantasy" route. It is safe, pastoral, and immediately establishes a "good" pantheon capable of benevolent creation. However, it feels derivative—telling players they are in "Furiotre" with a "Lumina" and "Terranor" doesn't differentiate us from a thousand other D&D settings. It lacks a specific hook.

**Version B** is the strongest aesthetically. The imagery of the sleeping entity falling and its body parts becoming the geography is visceral and unique. It sets a tone of melancholy and instability that suggests a world built on trauma rather than order. However, it is purely poetic; it lacks functional mechanics for the Magic System.

**Version C** is the "High Concept" trap. It feels more like a sci-fi origin than a myth. The idea of "World Eggs" is overused in modern fantasy, and the logic of "building a palace to have a home" feels weak for cosmic entities.

**Version D** offers the most mechanical utility. The "Anger becomes Light/Mountain" concept provides a clear source of conflict and a functional magic system (using emotion as fuel) without needing to invent new rules.

I vote for Version D.

Here is why: It is the only version that provides actual motivation for creation. In Versions A, B, and C, creation happens because the gods are bored, or sleeping, or need a home. That feels a bit too administrative for a creation myth.

In Version D, we have **Otre**, and he is *angry*. He is a god with a personality—specifically, a bad temper. People like angry gods; it makes them feel relatable. It also explains why the world is the way it is. The mountain (Ghaulen) is smoking because his rage never fully cooled down. The creation isn't a gift or a random accident; it's a tantrum. It sets a tone of struggle and emotion right from the opening line. It feels like a story, not a Wikipedia entry.

Critic 2:
I have to disagree. Version D is too aggressive for a myth meant to explain the beginning; it feels like a villain origin story, not a creation myth.

I prefer Version E. The imagery of the **world-eggs** hatching is classic and evocative. It immediately establishes a sense of structure and destiny ("Fates") which gives the world weight.

More importantly, look at the conflict: Oath versus Conflict. The idea that the conflict was resolved but resulted in a split—the life gods having a "nemesis" or a darker, colder sibling—introduces a duality that feels very ancient. It explains why the world has opposing forces (Day/Night, Good/Evil) not because of a temper tantrum, but because of a fundamental flaw in the design ("an oversight so narrow"). It creates a sense of tragic inevitability that I find much more compelling for this project.

Senior Editor:
Gentlemen, both of you have made strong points. Critic 1, you want emotional resonance and a driven protagonist. Critic 2, you want structural elegance and the introduction of complex duality.

samples.text:
I’m not sure this story’s about the beginning; I think it’s about the aftermath of a mistake. “The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories.” If that’s the head-note, the myth should begin with something that already looks like a history—something that’s a record, or a scar, or a trace.

A does that. It doesn’t start with a creature or a light or a breath; it starts with a sound that has no source and no destination. That’s already a history. The Hum is not an origin; it’s a before-that-never-arrived. And then it “wavers.” That’s not a generative act; it’s a failure. The First Accident. That’s a strong hinge word.

Velsha is the hinge. You give it a double meaning: “mistake” and “marrow.” That’s clever and it’s true to theme. A myth that begins with a mistake can carry all sorts of later histories that are structurally flawed. And the deities are not benevolent creators; they’re responses to a structural error. Orrumai is “the Architect of Spines” and “ribcage with no body.” Tessavar is “warm unraveling.” Those are not wholesome archetypes; they’re anatomical metaphors for a world that keeps coming apart.

The prose is precise. “Curdled into something new” is a great image, and “potential with a terrible itch” is chilling. It’s visceral without being grotesque. It feels like a single author’s voice, not a committee’s.

But there’s a risk. The myth could drift into abstraction. The world name “Furiotre” has a hard edge; if the myth is too cerebral, we’ll feel the disconnect. And if every subsequent creation story follows this tone of structural failure, the mythology might feel uniformly bleak.

instruct.prompt:
Here are several continuations of the same creation-myth opening.

Opening: The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning,

A. there was only the Hum — a single, droning note that stretched across the emptiness like a wire pulled taut between two points of nothing. It had no source and no destination. It simply *was*, and had always been, and would have continued forever had it not, in one inexplicable moment, wavered.

That waver was the First Accident.

The Hum split into two tones: one rising, one falling. Where they pulled apart, the space between them curdled into something new — a pale, trembling substance the old texts call **velsha**, which means both "mistake" and "marrow." Velsha was neither solid nor liquid nor light. It was *potential* with a terrible itch.

From the rising tone came **Orrumai**, the Architect of Spines. She was a being of impossible geometry — a ribcage with no body, an eye with no skull to house it, fingers that branched and branched again like winter trees. She did not think as mortals think. She *structured*. Where her attention fell, velsha hardened into bone-white stone, into the great latticed pillars that would become the bones of the world.

From the falling tone came **Tessavar**, the Warm Unraveling. Where Orrumai was sharp, Tessavar was soft — a creature of heat, decay, and tender dissolution.

B. nothing was as we know it. Each and every world-egg, the spheres that hold, nurture, and decide a plane's life span and possibility was hatched from the void. In the span of what Furiotre could consider an afternoon, in was torn apart by a war its first borns would sometimes refer to as the War of Fates. It started when the hatchlings awoke from the womb. Most clung to their eggs, but the few wake too soon or too late perished in the void.

The remaining 27 hatched from their shells soon, and were raised together. At the end of a year they grew into adults, and chose each of the Void's potentials to become their charges. Nilo, the goddess of all beginnings, knew of no flaws in the Gods' designs. It was the war that brought about her downfall. An oversight so narrow, that it left her to face the battle alone.

The life-gods brought conflict and the goddesses placed Oath to end it. Parsonering each other, the life-gods chose to temper their spirits. Their consciousness split and an other became them, colder, crueler, more miserable than their given sibling. Soon, every Life god had a nemesis, and the first dark pantheon was born.

C. there was only Otre, and Otre was angry.

He did not know why. He had woken in the dark between nothing and nothing with his fists already clenched and his teeth already grinding, and a heat already rising in him like a tide. He knew only that something had been done to him, or that something had been taken, or that something had been promised and never given. The reason was gone, but the anger remained, and it was so vast that it had nowhere to go.

So Otre raged, and his rage became the first light.

It was a red light, and it burned for an age. By its glow Otre searched the dark for the thing that had wronged him, but there was nothing there. There was no enemy to strike and no thief to chase. There was only himself, and his fury, and a silence that would not answer.

*Perhaps,* thought Otre, *I am angry because the dark is empty.*

So he tore a piece of his anger loose and hurled it down, and it cooled into stone. It became the first mountain, Ghaulen, which still smokes to this day. But when Otre looked upon it, his anger did not lessen. This was not the reason.

*Perhaps I am angry because the stone is alone.*

So he flung down more of himself.

D. the world was a blank slate, untouched by any sentient beings, only four great entities dwelled here. They were known as the Infinite Pantheon, the greatest beings in existence, who would go on to shape all of Furiotre as we know it.

Furiotre was not, at first, the home of the gods. There was no place for them here, no need for them to exist here. But one day, the Infinite Pantheon decided to take this strange world as a home for themselves. With all that they had, they built an expansive and magnificent palace, which they would call Altair, and then, over the years, they created all manner of beings to serve their purposes.

When they had finished their work, they decided to choose one of their own to rule over Altair, as there was no real need for any of them to leave, having no place to go. They also decided that each of them should take one child to carry on their line, and so they began to choose those who would lead the world they had created.

This new form of life they had created was beautiful and awe-inspiring, and they soon became known as the Children of the Infinite Pantheon, or simply The Children. There were dozens of them, each one more beautiful than the next, and they were chosen from among the vast array of beings the Infinite Pantheon had created.

E. there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet to hide the light. There was no silence, for nothing had yet learned to speak. There was only a great, sleeping creature whose name has been forgotten, and whose dreams had nowhere to go.

Then the creature dreamed of falling.

Its fear became the first sea.

It dreamed of catching itself, and its outstretched hands became the land. Between its fingers lay narrow straits; upon its knuckles rose mountains. The deepest valleys of Furiotre are said to be the creases of those ancient palms.

Still it fell.

So it dreamed of wings, and the wings became the sky. Their feathers scattered into stars, except for one, which caught fire and became the sun. Another fell into the sea, where it cooled into the moon. This is why the moon draws the waters upward: they remember the warmth it once brought them.

At last the creature dreamed of a place to stand.

From that dream grew the First Tree, whose roots pierced the land and whose branches held the sky apart. The creature settled beneath it and, for the first time, slept without fear.

But peaceful dreams are brief, even for the oldest things.

In its sleep, the creature heard a sound it had not made.

Three beings stood beside the sea. One had a face of white clay. One wore a cloak of living moths.

F. there was only the vast, swirling Abyss, an endless expanse of primal chaos and darkness. From this abyss emerged the First Breath, a gentle whisper that carried with it the seeds of creation. The whisper danced through the void, weaving patterns of light and shadow, and in its wake, it left the embryonic forms of the first deities.

The first to awaken was Lumina, the Goddess of Light, who brought forth the radiant stars and kindled the great sun, Illor. Her brilliant glow pierced the darkness, revealing the hidden wonders of Furiotre. With her arrival, warmth and life began to stir.

Next came Terranor, the Titan of Earth, who shaped the lands and mountains with his mighty hands. From his touch, rivers and valleys emerged, and he sowed the world with the seeds of vast forests, which danced under Lumina's guiding light.

As the world took form, Zephyra, the Mistress of Winds, emerged, painting the skies with rolling clouds and tender breezes. Her breath caressed the land, encouraging the sprouting seeds to grow and play, while guiding the golden leaves on their journey.

From the deepest depths of the Abyss rose Marinis, the Guardian of Waters. With a wave of her hand, the oceans, lakes, and rivers swelled into existence, teeming with creatures that shimmered like jewels against the sunlit surface.

Opening: The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning,

A. there was only the Hum — a single, droning note that stretched across the emptiness like a wire pulled taut between two points of nothing. It had no source and no destination. It simply *was*, and had always been, and would have continued forever had it not, in one inexplicable moment, wavered.

That waver was the First Accident.

The Hum split into two tones: one rising, one falling. Where they pulled apart, the space between them curdled into something new — a pale, trembling substance the old texts call **velsha**, which means both "mistake" and "marrow." Velsha was neither solid nor liquid nor light. It was *potential* with a terrible itch.

From the rising tone came **Orrumai**, the Architect of Spines. She was a being of impossible geometry — a ribcage with no body, an eye with no skull to house it, fingers that branched and branched again like winter trees. She did not think as mortals think. She *structured*. Where her attention fell, velsha hardened into bone-white stone, into the great latticed pillars that would become the bones of the world.

From the falling tone came **Tessavar**, the Warm Unraveling. Where Orrumai was sharp, Tessavar was soft — a creature of heat, decay, and tender dissolution.

B. nothing was as we know it. Each and every world-egg, the spheres that hold, nurture, and decide a plane's life span and possibility was hatched from the void. In the span of what Furiotre could consider an afternoon, in was torn apart by a war its first borns would sometimes refer to as the War of Fates. It started when the hatchlings awoke from the womb. Most clung to their eggs, but the few wake too soon or too late perished in the void.

The remaining 27 hatched from their shells soon, and were raised together. At the end of a year they grew into adults, and chose each of the Void's potentials to become their charges. Nilo, the goddess of all beginnings, knew of no flaws in the Gods' designs. It was the war that brought about her downfall. An oversight so narrow, that it left her to face the battle alone.

The life-gods brought conflict and the goddesses placed Oath to end it. Parsonering each other, the life-gods chose to temper their spirits. Their consciousness split and an other became them, colder, crueler, more miserable than their given sibling. Soon, every Life god had a nemesis, and the first dark pantheon was born.

C. there was only Otre, and Otre was angry.

He did not know why. He had woken in the dark between nothing and nothing with his fists already clenched and his teeth already grinding, and a heat already rising in him like a tide. He knew only that something had been done to him, or that something had been taken, or that something had been promised and never given. The reason was gone, but the anger remained, and it was so vast that it had nowhere to go.

So Otre raged, and his rage became the first light.

It was a red light, and it burned for an age. By its glow Otre searched the dark for the thing that had wronged him, but there was nothing there. There was no enemy to strike and no thief to chase. There was only himself, and his fury, and a silence that would not answer.

*Perhaps,* thought Otre, *I am angry because the dark is empty.*

So he tore a piece of his anger loose and hurled it down, and it cooled into stone. It became the first mountain, Ghaulen, which still smokes to this day. But when Otre looked upon it, his anger did not lessen. This was not the reason.

*Perhaps I am angry because the stone is alone.*

So he flung down more of himself.

D. the world was a blank slate, untouched by any sentient beings, only four great entities dwelled here. They were known as the Infinite Pantheon, the greatest beings in existence, who would go on to shape all of Furiotre as we know it.

Furiotre was not, at first, the home of the gods. There was no place for them here, no need for them to exist here. But one day, the Infinite Pantheon decided to take this strange world as a home for themselves. With all that they had, they built an expansive and magnificent palace, which they would call Altair, and then, over the years, they created all manner of beings to serve their purposes.

When they had finished their work, they decided to choose one of their own to rule over Altair, as there was no real need for any of them to leave, having no place to go. They also decided that each of them should take one child to carry on their line, and so they began to choose those who would lead the world they had created.

This new form of life they had created was beautiful and awe-inspiring, and they soon became known as the Children of the Infinite Pantheon, or simply The Children. There were dozens of them, each one more beautiful than the next, and they were chosen from among the vast array of beings the Infinite Pantheon had created.

E. there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet to hide the light. There was no silence, for nothing had yet learned to speak. There was only a great, sleeping creature whose name has been forgotten, and whose dreams had nowhere to go.

Then the creature dreamed of falling.

Its fear became the first sea.

It dreamed of catching itself, and its outstretched hands became the land. Between its fingers lay narrow straits; upon its knuckles rose mountains. The deepest valleys of Furiotre are said to be the creases of those ancient palms.

Still it fell.

So it dreamed of wings, and the wings became the sky. Their feathers scattered into stars, except for one, which caught fire and became the sun. Another fell into the sea, where it cooled into the moon. This is why the moon draws the waters upward: they remember the warmth it once brought them.

At last the creature dreamed of a place to stand.

From that dream grew the First Tree, whose roots pierced the land and whose branches held the sky apart. The creature settled beneath it and, for the first time, slept without fear.

But peaceful dreams are brief, even for the oldest things.

In its sleep, the creature heard a sound it had not made.

Three beings stood beside the sea. One had a face of white clay. One wore a cloak of living moths.

F. there was only the vast, swirling Abyss, an endless expanse of primal chaos and darkness. From this abyss emerged the First Breath, a gentle whisper that carried with it the seeds of creation. The whisper danced through the void, weaving patterns of light and shadow, and in its wake, it left the embryonic forms of the first deities.

The first to awaken was Lumina, the Goddess of Light, who brought forth the radiant stars and kindled the great sun, Illor. Her brilliant glow pierced the darkness, revealing the hidden wonders of Furiotre. With her arrival, warmth and life began to stir.

Next came Terranor, the Titan of Earth, who shaped the lands and mountains with his mighty hands. From his touch, rivers and valleys emerged, and he sowed the world with the seeds of vast forests, which danced under Lumina's guiding light.

As the world took form, Zephyra, the Mistress of Winds, emerged, painting the skies with rolling clouds and tender breezes. Her breath caressed the land, encouraging the sprouting seeds to grow and play, while guiding the golden leaves on their journey.

From the deepest depths of the Abyss rose Marinis, the Guardian of Waters. With a wave of her hand, the oceans, lakes, and rivers swelled into existence, teeming with creatures that shimmered like jewels against the sunlit surface.

Which one has the best texture and feel, the one that reads as if it were told rather than assembled? Reply with the letter on the first line, then one or two sentences on why.
instruct.text: A. This continuation has a poetic and mythic quality, with rich imagery and a sense of ancient mystery. The descriptions are vivid and engaging, allowing the reader to feel as though they are listening to an old tale passed down through generations.

Most clung to their eggs, but the few wake too soon or too late perished in the void.

The remaining 27 hatched from their shells soon, and were raised together. At the end of a year they grew into adults, and chose each of the Void's potentials to become their charges. Nilo, the goddess of all beginnings, knew of no flaws in the Gods' designs. It was the war that brought about her downfall. An oversight so narrow, that it left her to face the battle alone.

The life-gods brought conflict and the goddesses placed Oath to end it. Parsonering each other, the life-gods chose to temper their spirits. Their consciousness split and an other became them, colder, crueler, more miserable than their given sibling. Soon, every Life god had a nemesis, and the first dark pantheon was born.

C. there was only Otre, and Otre was angry.

He did not know why. He had woken in the dark between nothing and nothing with his fists already clenched and his teeth already grinding, and a heat already rising in him like a tide. He knew only that something had been done to him, or that something had been taken, or that something had been promised and never given. The reason was gone, but the anger remained, and it was so vast that it had nowhere to go.

So Otre raged, and his rage became the first light.

It was a red light, and it burned for an age. By its glow Otre searched the dark for the thing that had wronged him, but there was nothing there. There was no enemy to strike and no thief to chase. There was only himself, and his fury, and a silence that would not answer.

*Perhaps,* thought Otre, *I am angry because the dark is empty.*

So he tore a piece of his anger loose and hurled it down, and it cooled into stone. It became the first mountain, Ghaulen, which still smokes to this day. But when Otre looked upon it, his anger did not lessen. This was not the reason.

*Perhaps I am angry because the stone is alone.*

So he flung down more of himself.

D. the world was a blank slate, untouched by any sentient beings, only four great entities dwelled here. They were known as the Infinite Pantheon, the greatest beings in existence, who would go on to shape all of Furiotre as we know it.

Furiotre was not, at first, the home of the gods. There was no place for them here, no need for them to exist here. But one day, the Infinite Pantheon decided to take this strange world as a home for themselves. With all that they had, they built an expansive and magnificent palace, which they would call Altair, and then, over the years, they created all manner of beings to serve their purposes.

When they had finished their work, they decided to choose one of their own to rule over Altair, as there was no real need for any of them to leave, having no place to go. They also decided that each of them should take one child to carry on their line, and so they began to choose those who would lead the world they had created.

This new form of life they had created was beautiful and awe-inspiring, and they soon became known as the Children of the Infinite Pantheon, or simply The Children. There were dozens of them, each one more beautiful than the next, and they were chosen from among the vast array of beings the Infinite Pantheon had created.

E. there was no darkness, for there was nothing yet to hide the light. There was no silence, for nothing had yet learned to speak. There was only a great, sleeping creature whose name has been forgotten, and whose dreams had nowhere to go.

Then the creature dreamed of falling.

Its fear became the first sea.

It dreamed of catching itself, and its outstretched hands became the land. Between its fingers lay narrow straits; upon its knuckles rose mountains. The deepest valleys of Furiotre are said to be the creases of those ancient palms.

Still it fell.

So it dreamed of wings, and the wings became the sky. Their feathers scattered into stars, except for one, which caught fire and became the sun. Another fell into the sea, where it cooled into the moon. This is why the moon draws the waters upward: they remember the warmth it once brought them.

At last the creature dreamed of a place to stand.

From that dream grew the First Tree, whose roots pierced the land and whose branches held the sky apart. The creature settled beneath it and, for the first time, slept without fear.

But peaceful dreams are brief, even for the oldest things.

In its sleep, the creature heard a sound it had not made.

Three beings stood beside the sea. One had a face of white clay. One wore a cloak of living moths.

F. there was only the vast, swirling Abyss, an endless expanse of primal chaos and darkness. From this abyss emerged the First Breath, a gentle whisper that carried with it the seeds of creation. The whisper danced through the void, weaving patterns of light and shadow, and in its wake, it left the embryonic forms of the first deities.

The first to awaken was Lumina, the Goddess of Light, who brought forth the radiant stars and kindled the great sun, Illor. Her brilliant glow pierced the darkness, revealing the hidden wonders of Furiotre. With her arrival, warmth and life began to stir.

Next came Terranor, the Titan of Earth, who shaped the lands and mountains with his mighty hands. From his touch, rivers and valleys emerged, and he sowed the world with the seeds of vast forests, which danced under Lumina's guiding light.

As the world took form, Zephyra, the Mistress of Winds, emerged, painting the skies with rolling clouds and tender breezes. Her breath caressed the land, encouraging the sprouting seeds to grow and play, while guiding the golden leaves on their journey.

From the deepest depths of the Abyss rose Marinis, the Guardian of Waters. With a wave of her hand, the oceans, lakes, and rivers swelled into existence, teeming with creatures that shimmered like jewels against the sunlit surface.

Which one has the best texture and feel, the one that reads as if it were told rather than assembled? Reply with the letter on the first line, then one or two sentences on why.
instruct.text:
E

It has the cadence of oral myth: short, rhythmic beats ("Still it fell."), dream-logic cause and effect, and folk explanations like "This is why the moon draws the waters upward" and "are said to be the creases of those ancient palms." These make it feel handed down rather than designed. C comes close with its repeating "Perhaps I am angry because…" refrain, but E's world-shaping feels more lived-in and less like a list of inventions.
